title: Tool Use Around Water, Electricity, and Cultivation Equipment

content.overview: Cultivation rooms combine water delivery, drainage, pumps, lights, fans, environmental equipment, extension cords, benches, and frequent maintenance. A portable tool that is acceptable in a dry maintenance area may require different equipment or a different work plan where water or conductive liquids are present. Workers must recognize the interaction between the tool, the electrical environment, and the surrounding cultivation system before starting work.

vocabulary.definition: A work area where water or another conductive liquid can increase the likelihood that electrical current reaches a person or unintended path.
Portable equipment supplied through a flexible cord and attachment plug rather than fixed wiring.
A hazard created not by the tool alone but by the combination of tool, water, surfaces, utilities, people, and nearby equipment.

sections.title: Treat water as a planning variable
sections.body: OSHA's electrical equipment-use rule states that portable electric equipment and flexible cords used in highly conductive locations or where employees are likely to contact water or conductive liquids must be approved for those locations. This means the worker should not simply wipe the floor and assume any portable tool is acceptable. Determine whether the environment, equipment approval, connection method, and facility procedure support the task. If there is uncertainty, stop and escalate to the person responsible for electrical or maintenance safety.

sections.title: Inspect cords and connections before the task
sections.body: Cord-and-plug equipment and extension cords must be visually inspected before use on a shift for external defects and evidence of possible internal damage. Look for damaged jackets, loose parts, missing or deformed pins, crushed or pinched areas, or other visible conditions that affect safe use. Do not use cords to raise or lower equipment, and do not route or fasten them in ways that damage insulation. Keep connections and routing out of foreseeable irrigation, drainage, cart, and pinch paths.

sections.title: Coordinate with operating cultivation systems
sections.body: Maintenance can create secondary hazards when pumps start, benches move, irrigation opens, lights cycle, or another worker energizes nearby equipment. Define what equipment must remain off, what zones must stay dry, who controls the work area, and how unexpected system operation will be handled. The correct control may be rescheduling the task, using different equipment, isolating a system under the facility procedure, or involving qualified maintenance personnel. A cultivation technician should recognize the conflict and escalate rather than improvise electrical work outside authorization.

workedExamples: A repair requires a portable electric tool beside an active drain where irrigation water is expected. The technician stops to verify equipment approval and facility electrical controls rather than assuming a normal dry-area setup is adequate.
An extension cord crosses beneath a rolling bench and has visible flattening. It is removed from use and the task is rerouted instead of placing tape over the damaged section.
commonMistakes: Treating water as only a slip hazard while ignoring its interaction with electrical equipment.
Inspecting the tool but not its cord, plug, extension cord, or routing path.
Performing unauthorized electrical troubleshooting because the cultivation task seems simple.
content.practicalApplication: Map a simulated maintenance task in a grow room. Mark water sources, drains, electrical connections, moving equipment, cord routes, and people. Identify which conditions can be controlled locally and which require maintenance/electrical escalation before the tool may be used.
content.summary: Tool safety in cultivation depends on the surrounding system. Portable electrical equipment, cords, water, drainage, and operating facility equipment must be evaluated together, with unsafe or uncertain conditions escalated before work begins.
